english: For each real number $\lambda\ne7$, the system of equations
has a unique solution $(x_\lambda,y_\lambda,z_\lambda)$. Then $\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to7}y_\lambda$ is equal to
hindi: प्रत्येक वास्तविक संख्या $\lambda\ne7$ के लिए समीकरण निकाय
का एक अद्वितीय हल $(x_\lambda,y_\lambda,z_\lambda)$ है। तब $\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to7}y_\lambda$ बराबर है
solution_full: Coefficient determinant: $\Delta=1(2\lambda-12)-1(\lambda-3)+1(4-2)=\lambda-7$, non-zero for $\lambda\ne7$, so Cramer's rule applies.
Let $c=\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+12$. Replacing the second column by the constants: $\Delta_2=\begin{vmatrix}1&3&1\\1&6&3\\1&c&\lambda\end{vmatrix}=1(6\lambda-3c)-3(\lambda-3)+1(c-6)=3\lambda-2c+3$.
At $\lambda=7$ itself $\Delta=0$ and the system has infinitely many solutions (the constant becomes $12=3\cdot6-2\cdot3$); the limit picks out the solution $(7,-11,7)$ of that line.
originality_note: New: the limit of a Cramer quotient at the parameter where the coefficient determinant vanishes; numerator and denominator share the factor (lambda - 7), and the limit selects one point of the solution line of the singular system (way 4). Closest known: finding lambda for unique, no or infinitely many solutions. Different because: the question asks for the limiting solution, not the classification.

concept_use.Cramer's rule: y = Delta_2/Delta by Cramer's rule; both determinants contain the factor lambda - 7, which cancels before the limit.

stem_review: Read as a student: lambda real and not 7, the unique solution exists because Delta = lambda - 7; the limit is of a well-defined function. Checked with sympy: solution (lambda, 3-2 lambda, lambda). Answer -11 at (B) as planned. Changed: No change.
key_step: Cramer's rule gives y = Delta_2/Delta = 3 - 2 lambda after cancelling lambda - 7.
justification: Two 3x3 determinants and a cancellation, then a direct limit; routine multi-step. Comparable to 2023-P1-Q14 (L1) on systems, but the limiting step adds a stage, so L2.
